extracted.intended_audience: writers, MFA faculty, MFA students, and readers concerned with diversity and pedagogy in creative-writing programs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for assessing the racial inclusiveness and pedagogical practices of MFA programs and writing workshops, and for how writers (especially white writers) should engage in conversations about race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty breadth in literary traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: One key issue here is whether the faculty in MFA programs is well versed in a variety of literary traditions and thought?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts his PhD experience (reading a handful of Amiri Baraka poems) with an MFA that taught nothing about African American letters, Asian American, Native American, Latino American, global writing, or postcolonial theory. Evaluate programs by whether faculty teach and know multiple literary traditions and perspectives rather than a narrow, white-centered canon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of people-of-color literary traditions in curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Many students at VONA and other writers of color express an absence in their MFA training and thus, in the faculty that teach in these programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit curricular attention to African American, Asian American, Native American, Latino American, global, and postcolonial literatures; absence of such attention is an indicator of systemic exclusion rather than isolated oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine default whiteness in literary practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The default literary practice in American writing is that white writers do not have to identify their white characters as being white. Is this practice politically and racially neutral or is it a practice which can be examined in light of a literary and political critique?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether workshops interrogate implicit norms (like treating whiteness as unmarked). A healthy program should be able to acknowledge multiple valid perspectives on such practices rather than treating them as neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't dismiss racial critique as 'too political' or 'PC'
rubrics_metrics.description: In most current MFA workshops, what would happen if such a critique were expressed? Would it be acknowledged that there are actually at least two sides... Or would such a critique be dismissed as too political, as 'PC' and therefore not literary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A red flag is dismissing structural/racial critiques as merely 'political' and therefore illegitimate. Programs should allow and engage with politically-inflected literary critiques rather than excluding them from being 'literary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hominem and language-based dismissal of POC critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: When the person of color brings up a critique, the response is often to critique the so-called character or personality faults of that person or to critique the language in which the critique is expressed (too angry, uses too many swear words, the person doesn’t have the right to make this critique because he or she is in some other way privileged, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These responses are used by dominant culture to dismiss concrete and systemic issues. Evaluations should note whether discussions resort to attacking the messenger or their tone instead of addressing the substance of critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize mechanisms that silence critique
rubrics_metrics.description: One way in which power exercises itself is by keeping critiques of the dominant power from ever being voiced. Ad hominem attacks are one such way, ignoring the existence of the critiques are another (i.e., not knowing the literary traditions and thought of people of color), and standard practices of how workshops are run yet another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether institutional or pedagogical practices (what is taught, how workshops are run, who gets heard) function to exclude or silence critiques about race and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: White participants should begin by listening and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are really interested in having a true conversation about race with people of color, then you should realize that historically this has been a mainly one-sided conversation. ... perhaps the role for you as an individual white person is, at first, simply to listen, to find out what you don’t know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate individual conduct: white writers/teachers should demonstrate curiosity, humility, and willingness to learn rather than assuming they already understand; acknowledge 'things we don’t know we don’t know.' Listening is an active skill and part of good conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid burdening writers of color with educating others
rubrics_metrics.description: VONA ... provides a space where writers of color don’t have to spend a majority of the workshop explaining their work or their lives to white writers or arguing with white writers about our right to tell our truths and lives in our own voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should structure workshops so POC are not required to spend disproportionate time justifying or explaining their experiences; assess workload of emotional/educational labor placed on POC participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide both safe spaces for POC and mixed workshops on race
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Stonecoast MFA program, Alexs Pate and I teach a workshop, 'Writing About Race.' ... I also teach at the VONA Voices Writers’ Workshop, a writers’ conference for writers of color taught by writers of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: offer dedicated spaces for writers of color to develop without constant racial explanation, and also offer structured, facilitated mixed workshops (with explicit safety and pedagogical framing) where white writers and POC can discuss race productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge historical asymmetry in narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Richard Wright has indicated that white and black Americans are engaged in a struggle over the description of reality. But one key difference is that that white description has prevailed and dominated our society and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs and participants should be evaluated on whether they recognize that racial narratives have been historically unequal, and whether they take steps to correct for that dominance rather than assuming a level playing field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening may require identity revision; be prepared to change
rubrics_metrics.description: In Baldwin’s The Devil Finds Work... encountering that stranger... should cause one to question one’s identity... you have to listen to the stranger, you have to learn from the stranger. And that requires you, said Baldwin, to change your robes, to reconstruct your identity. Listening then is dangerous, threatening. But... necessary and life affirming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether individuals and programs foster real openness to being changed by others’ perspectives rather than token acknowledgment; true listening implies willingness to revise one’s self-understanding.
